beats.narration_text: There's a line every LLM practitioner has heard: set temperature to zero for deterministic output. Let's check that against actual code instead of taking it on faith.

props.topic: TERMINAL COMMAND · NOT A CLAUDE RESPONSE
output: Beat 2: temperature=0 is refused, not treated as a deterministic mode
Raised ValueError: Need logits and a positive finite temperature

beats.narration_text: Here's the stakes. Plenty of production systems are built on the assumption that a temperature of zero means the model just picks the top answer, every time, no sampling involved. If that assumption is wrong, anywhere you rely on it — reproducible test suites, deterministic pipelines, cached responses keyed on identical output — is quietly built on sand. The chapter's own reference implementation gives a very direct way to check the assumption: try it.
beats.visual_intent: Plain text card, no chart yet: the claim "temperature 0 = deterministic" presented as something to test, not something asserted as true.

beats.role_note: ClaudeCodeBeat — actual reference implementation, trimmed to the lines that teach
beats.narration_text: Here's why it fails. Read the guard clause: if temperature is not finite, or temperature is less than or equal to zero, the function refuses outright, before it computes anything. Zero isn't a special case this function recognizes as 'be deterministic.' It's excluded input. Whatever deterministic selection would look like, this is not that operation.

props.title: main.py — reference implementation
props.code:
def probabilities(logits, temperature=1.0):
    if not logits or not math.isfinite(temperature) or temperature <= 0:
        raise ValueError("Need logits and a positive finite temperature")
    if not all(math.isfinite(x) for x in logits):
        raise ValueError("Logits must be finite")
    peak = max(logits)
    weights = [math.exp((x - peak) / temperature) for x in logits]
    total = sum(weights)
    return [weight / total for weight in weights]

# temperature <= 0 is refused BEFORE any exponential is computed.
# This is an exclusion, not a deterministic mode.

beats.role_note: Manim — real ValueError, then real sample() counts at T=0.5
beats.narration_text: Run it. Real output: a ValueError, not a number. So back off to a low but positive temperature — one-half — and sample a thousand draws with a fixed seed. The top-scoring outcome gets about eighty-seven percent of the probability and wins eight hundred forty-nine of the thousand draws — matching the chapter's own published table exactly. But the other one hundred fifty-one draws didn't disappear. Concentrated is not the same as certain.
beats.visual_intent: First half: the real ValueError text rendered directly, in red, held for 2 seconds. Second half: bar chart from real counts {0:18, 1:133, 2:849} out of 1000, with assigned probabilities (1.6%, 11.7%, 86.7%) labeled beside each bar.

beats.narration_text: Check the output before trusting it. Concentration approaching eighty-seven percent is not the same claim as certainty. So build a genuine contrast: a function that's deterministic by definition — argmax_select doesn't sample at all, it just returns the top score, every time by construction. Then compare it against a temperature that only concentrates probability, and see how close the two can actually look.

props.command: python3 -c "from demo import argmax_select; print(argmax_select([1,2,3], count=1000))"
props.topic: TERMINAL COMMAND · NOT A CLAUDE RESPONSE

beats.role_note: Manim — sample() variance vs constructed argmax_select() zero variance, split screen, labeled
beats.narration_text: Here's the real contrast. On the left, sample at temperature one-half, one thousand draws — the variance from before. On the right, argmax_select: a function I wrote myself, not part of the chapter, that returns the top score's index by construction, every time. One thousand draws, one thousand identical results — guaranteed, not just likely. Sampling can produce that same result too, especially at lower temperatures — and it's worth checking whether that's a coincidence of this run, or something built into the definition.
beats.visual_intent: Split-screen bar charts. Left: sample() counts {0:18, 1:133, 2:849}, visible variance across three bars. Right: argmax_select() counts {2:1000}, a single full bar, others at zero. Right side carries a held caption: CONSTRUCTED FOR THIS VIDEO — not in the chapter's code.

beats.role_note: lesson in one beat + named boundary
beats.narration_text: Temperature works through a ratio between scores. As temperature shrinks, that ratio grows without limit — in exact math, every outcome keeps a positive probability, so the distribution never quite becomes one-hot. In practice, though, a run of many draws can land on the same outcome every time by chance, and in real floating-point code, low enough temperatures make the other probabilities underflow to exactly zero — so the actual numbers you get can become identical to argmax's, even though the operation that produced them is different. One more thing this doesn't establish: what an actual product's temperature-zero setting does.
beats.visual_intent: Plain text, no chart: the ratio formula p_i/p_k = exp((z_i - z_k)/T), then below it, the boundary statement as a separate card: "What this doesn't establish."

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — prompt READ aloud AND discussed; greeting 'Your turn.'
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Clone the repo, run main.py, then run this: try your own scores at a low temperature, like point-oh-one, and see whether the counts come back identical. They probably will — check whether that's a coincidence of the sample, or the floating-point numbers themselves underflowing to zero. Read the boundary out loud before you conclude anything about a real product from a teaching toy.

props.command: python3 -c "from main import sample; print(sample([<your scores>], count=1000, seed=7, temperature=<your low T>))"

beats.narration_text: Low Temperature Is Not Argmax. Here's what the run actually showed. Temperature zero is refused by the reference implementation, not treated as deterministic. At one-half, one outcome gets about eighty-seven percent of the probability, and the other two still won one hundred fifty-one of a thousand draws. Argmax_select is deterministic by construction; sampling can look that way at lower temperatures. And none of this says how a real product handles temperature zero, or where your own numbers would underflow. Run the code — don't just trust the slogan.
